title: Hazel and the Undertow
premise: Emrys Kavanagh, a bridge inspector who measures everything and feels nothing he can quantify, discovers a box of undelivered letters behind his late mother's wardrobe — letters from his father, presumed dead for thirty years, addressed to an address in the old riverside neighborhood scheduled for demolition. As Emrys reads them and retraces his father's final months, he uncovers that his mother's silence was not grief but a choice: she had known her husband was alive, and had chosen loyalty to a version of the truth over the man himself. The last chapter brings Emrys to the neighborhood's final day before rerouting, where he finds his elderly father living under another name; forgiveness arrives not as reconciliation but as recognition, and Emrys leaves owning his own life at last.
about_author: Jude Underhill is the pen name of a former municipal surveyor who spent eleven years inspecting bridges along industrial river corridors before turning to fiction. Their stories examine the quiet architecture of families — what holds, what corrodes, and who gets blamed when something gives way.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Emrys inspects the Kellerman Bridge, cataloguing hairline fractures with the same detachment he applies to his marriage. POV: Emrys. The emotional beat is numbness disguised as competence — a man who trusts measurements because they never lie back.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Clearing his mother's house after her funeral, Emrys pries loose a warped panel and finds forty-one unopened letters, all postmarked within a single year, all addressed in his father's hand. POV: Emrys. The beat is vertigo: the past refusing to stay load-bearing.

chapters.title: The First Letter
chapters.summary: Emrys reads the earliest letter — tender, apologetic, dated three months after the funeral that never happened. His wife Nell watches him change. POV: Emrys, with a brief letter-voice interlude. The beat is betrayal's first cold draft under a closed door.

chapters.title: Nell's Ledger
chapters.summary: Nell confronts Emrys about his distance, revealing her own secret: she has been offered a job abroad and hasn't told him. POV: Nell. The beat is mirrored concealment — two tenants in one house, each hiding a lease termination.

chapters.title: The Old Neighborhood
chapters.summary: Emrys visits the condemned riverside district where the letters were sent, meeting Dolores, a former neighbor who recognizes the name Kavanagh and goes quiet. POV: Emrys. The beat is the past pushing back — doors opening onto rooms someone wants kept shut.

chapters.title: What Dolores Knows
chapters.summary: Dolores admits she posted the letters back to Emrys's mother decades ago at his father's request, believing she was helping a reconciliation; instead she may have enabled a lifelong lie. POV: Dolores. The beat is guilt as inheritance — complicity passed down like a debt.

chapters.title: The Middle Letters
chapters.summary: Reading onward, Emrys learns his mother returned every letter unopened except one, and that his father stayed nearby for years, watching from a distance. POV: Emrys. The beat is rage curdling into grief — realizing loyalty and cruelty wore the same coat.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: The city announces the final bus route through the old neighborhood will be discontinued; Nell accepts the job abroad and asks Emrys directly whether there is anything left to save. POV: Nell. The beat is ultimatum as mercy — love demanding honesty or nothing.

chapters.title: The Man Under Another Name
chapters.summary: On the route's second-to-last day, Emrys rides the old bus and finds his father — frail, renamed, tending a garden on the demolition list. They speak awkwardly across thirty years of invented death. POV: Emrys. The beat is the climax: truth standing exposed, neither man able to measure it.

chapters.title: Last Bus Out
chapters.summary: Emrys forgives not by absolving his parents but by refusing their arithmetic; he tells Nell everything and chooses to go with her, mailing his father one letter of his own. POV: Emrys. The beat is resolution as ownership — a tenant finally signing the deed to his own life.
